title: Roux
summary: Equal fat + flour cooked together — Louisiana gravies and French mother sauces.
origins: French technique documented in Marie-Antoine Carême's 19th-century sauce work; Louisiana Creole and Cajun cooks adapted it for gumbo, étouffée, and dark gravies. Each color — white, blond, brown, chocolate — adds nuttier flavor and thickening power.
history: Roux-thickened sauces define French classical cuisine and Gulf Coast cooking alike. Cajun dark roux can take 45+ minutes of stirring — a ritual, not a shortcut. Instant roux products appeared in Louisiana groceries in the late 1900s for weeknight gumbo.
first_known: Documented ~1800s French haute cuisine; Gulf Coast parallel traditions

timeline.event: Carême codifies roux in French sauce theory
Cajun dark roux tradition formalizes in Louisiana home kitchens
Jarred dry roux for faster gumbo

teaching: Equal parts fat and flour by weight — not volume.
Stir constantly once flour hits fat; burnt roux is bitter beyond saving.
Dark roux thickens less but flavors more — add okra or filé if too thin.
fun_fact: A chocolate-dark roux can take 45 minutes of stirring — Cajun cooks call it patience you can taste.
